title: Module 4 · Electronic Commerce, Fintech, and Trust Online
description: Interactive, case-led module on electronic commerce and fintech: what electronic commerce is, the electronic marketplace and disintermediation, business-to-consumer, business-to-business, consumer-to-consumer and e-government transactions, fintech and what it displaces, payment services and mobile and peer-to-peer payments, cryptocurrencies and blockchain, card-not-present risk, chargebacks, the card security code and fraud screening, consumer protection, online sales tax, intellectual property and digital rights management, with supplements on the platform, payment and fulfillment ecosystem behind a storefront and on turning the chapter into a written analysis.
brandSub: Module 4 · Trade, payment, and trust online
hero:
Module 4

Electronic Commerce, Fintech, and Trust Online

Modules 1 to 3 built the ground: what a system is, which one a company should build, and what all of it runs on. This module is about the moment money actually moves. Somebody you have never met, in a place you cannot see, sends you a payment for something you have not handed over yet — and both of you have to trust an arrangement neither of you built. Everything in this chapter is about how that trust is manufactured, what it costs, and who pays when it fails.

This module is built differently

The earlier modules explain first and practise second, and they explain at length. This one is roughly a third of the reading and about twice the practice, because this material is judgement rather than vocabulary. Nobody struggles with the definition of a chargeback. They struggle with deciding whether to ship the order.

  1. Every section carries a mini case. A short situation, a few facts, usually a small exhibit of figures, and two or three decisions to make. The debrief stays shut until you have answered all of them, so the point of the case is worked out rather than read.
  2. Read the short piece first, then work. The prose in each section is deliberately brief and exists to arm the activity that follows it, not to substitute for it.
  3. Every option explains itself. Including the ones you did not choose. Knowing why a plausible answer is wrong is the part that survives into the next case.
  4. Two supplements are labeled as such. The last two sections are applications, not textbook objectives. They connect this chapter to the services a real storefront runs on and to the written analysis this course asks for.
  5. Finish with the final challenge. Situations rather than definitions, scored by objective, so a weak area shows up instead of being averaged away.

Where this module sits in the course objectives

The modules follow the textbook’s learning objectives, but the course is graded against a different list of eleven. This table says plainly which of them this module serves and which it leaves to other work, so you always know why you are reading something.

Reach

Selling without a shop

Electronic commerce moved the transaction onto a network, and in doing so let a producer reach a customer directly — removing whoever used to stand between them.

Money

Paying without a bank branch

Fintech did the same thing to financial services: one job, done very well, reaching the customer without the institution that used to sit in the middle.

Risk

Trusting a stranger

No card to hold, no signature, no face. The merchant carries the loss when the transaction is disputed, so screening an order is a business decision, not a technical one.

Rules

Trading across borders

A single online storefront can fall under consumer protection, tax and intellectual property rules from places nobody at the company has ever been.

One idea connects the whole module Every arrangement in this chapter exists to replace a form of trust that used to be physical. A shop you can walk into, a card you can hold, a signature, a bank with a door on the street. Take those away and something has to stand in for them — a payment service, a public ledger, a risk score, a returns policy, a law. Each of those substitutes works, and each one costs somebody something. Most of the decisions in this module are about which cost to accept.

Reference

Chapter vocabulary

Every term the chapter defines, written so it makes sense on its own, with an example beside it. Search by word, or filter by the objective the term belongs to. Watch for the pairs that sound alike and are not: a payment service and a cryptocurrency, a chargeback and a refund, the card security code and the card number, a copyright and a trademark.
finalIntro:
Put it together

Final challenge

Situations rather than definitions. Each one puts you in front of a decision somebody actually has to make — ship it or hold it, absorb the fee or pass it on, comply or withdraw — and asks what is really going on. Every company described is invented. Answer all of them, then score: the result breaks out by objective, so a weak area points at a section to reread instead of disappearing into one number.
foot: What to do next. Buy something small online this week and watch the machinery instead of the product. Count the steps between wanting it and paying for it, and ask which of them exists to reduce your risk and which exists to reduce the seller’s. Notice who holds your card details at the end. Notice what the return policy actually promises, and where the seller says its jurisdiction is. Then ask the question this module keeps returning to: if this transaction goes wrong, whose money is it, and who decides?
